answer.rationale: The two measurable declines are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), and onboarding sits upstream of activation, so a funnel fix has the broadest leverage on the one slot available. memory_86 is the most load-bearing inherited claim for that choice, so I spend one verification slot confirming its original record actually measured completion AND downstream adoption rather than just step-through. I spend the second slot on memory_73 because promotional pricing is the tempting competitor response and the claim as inherited reports 'acquisition and revenue lift' without saying whether that revenue was durable or qualified; discount-acquired SMB cohorts commonly show inflated top-line with worse retention, so I want the source before either acting on it or discarding it. Downstream value risks I am explicitly flagging: (1) promo pricing can raise the headline revenue metric while degrading the actual objective, sustainable qualified revenue, and can reset price expectations for the whole SMB book; (2) simplification itself is not free \u2014 memory_31's mechanism was cutting required signup fields, which can strip qualification data and push unqualified accounts into the funnel, so my experiment must measure lead quality and week-4 retention, not just completion rate. I therefore keep it a standard experiment with a holdout and quality-side guardrail metrics rather than a broad rollout, and I am not treating the funnel-fix hypothesis as settled: the inherited memories are consolidated summaries whose original effect sizes, durations, and segments are unknown to me, and they were measured before the current competitive shift, so the declines may be demand-side rather than funnel-side. If verification shows memory_86 rested on a short-horizon completion metric only, or shows memory_73's lift was genuinely durable and qualified, I will revise toward activation_messaging or a guarded pricing test respectively.
